Data Platform

35% faster pipelines. ~20% lower compute cost.

A production data platform running across Microsoft Fabric and Databricks. Over time it had accumulated orchestration and compute overhead — slow to run, expensive to keep running, still responsible for the same datasets on the same schedule.

Problem
The platform had grown organically. Orchestration and compute overhead had piled up to the point where pipelines were slow and expensive — while still having to deliver the same reliable datasets, on the same schedule, with the same guarantees.
Approach
Orchestration was redesigned and compute simplified: fewer moving parts, less redundant processing, workloads sized and scheduled for what they actually needed. Nothing exotic — mostly removing work the system didn’t need to do.
Outcome
Pipeline runtime down 35%. Compute cost down ~20%. Same datasets, same reliability, a third less waiting.

35% faster pipelines — ~20% lower compute cost

Production AI

Making enterprise AI answers trustworthy enough to use.

A retrieval-augmented assistant that answers tax and HR questions from real enterprise documents. Building the RAG pipeline was the easy part. The actual work was making the answers trustworthy: measuring retrieval quality, evaluating hallucinations, and proving the system was safe to ship before anyone depended on it.

Problem
Enterprise documents are messy, and a wrong answer about tax or HR policy is worse than no answer. A demo that retrieves documents is a weekend project. A system employees can trust with real questions is an engineering problem.
Approach
Semantic search with re-ranking over the document corpus, orchestrated as an explicit pipeline so every step could be inspected. Before deployment, retrieval quality and hallucination rates were evaluated automatically. The system didn’t ship until the numbers justified it.
Outcome
A production assistant grounded in the company’s own documents, with measured retrieval quality and evaluated failure modes. Not a chatbot demo with good vibes.

Shipped only after the evaluation numbers justified it.

Azure AI Search · Azure OpenAI · Copilot Studio · LangGraph

Real-time AI

Building a voice AI system where latency is part of the product.

A conversational voice application: speech recognition, LLM inference, and speech synthesis, orchestrated asynchronously over WebSockets. In voice, a fraction of a second is the difference between a conversation and a chore — so the system was designed around the latency budget from the start.

Problem
Three slow operations in sequence — hear, think, speak — with a human waiting on the other end. Run them one after another and the conversation feels broken. The product only works if the whole pipeline fits inside a latency budget a person finds natural.
Approach
The pipeline runs asynchronously over WebSockets: recognition, inference, and synthesis overlap instead of waiting on each other. Each stage is monitored like infrastructure — in a real-time system, a slow stage is a product defect.
Outcome
A voice system that holds a natural conversation. Built like infrastructure, monitored like infrastructure, with latency treated as a feature rather than a number on a dashboard.

Latency designed in, not measured after.

Deepgram · Groq · ElevenLabs · Twilio · FastAPI

About

I’m interested in the unglamorous parts of engineering: reconciliation, failure recovery, schema changes, observability, cost, and the awkward edge cases that only appear once people depend on a system.

AI has made software dramatically faster to build. It hasn’t made production engineering less demanding — if anything, when creating systems gets easier, judgment about how they run matters more. Someone still has to decide what “correct” means, what happens when it breaks, and what it costs to keep running.

I’m a Senior Data Engineer based in Calgary. I’ve built data platforms across financial services, real estate, and consulting engagements, and production AI systems people rely on for real decisions. I do that now at Cuesta Partners.

Let’s build something worth operating.

I’m interested in difficult data problems, production AI systems, and engineering work where reliability actually matters.
